entities.name: Bangladesh National Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Bangladesh National Museum (বাংলাদেশ জাতীয় জাদুঘর), established in 1913 as the Dhaka Museum under British colonial rule and renamed after Bangladesh's independence (1971), is the largest and most comprehensive museum in Bangladesh — holding approximately 83,000 items spanning archaeological artifacts from the ancient Bengal region, Islamic art from the Mughal and Sultanate periods, natural history, and contemporary Bangladeshi art — and representing Bangladesh's effort to construct a national cultural identity from Bengal's extraordinarily rich but multiply-claimed heritage.

Bangladesh's national heritage narrative is politically complex: its territory encompasses the eastern half of the ancient Bengal region, which has been variously claimed by Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist, and Bengali nationalist frameworks. The museum's collection reflects pre-Islamic Hindu and Buddhist sculpture from the Pala dynasty (8th-12th centuries), which ruled Bengal during the period when Nalanda and Vikramashila universities flourished — making eastern Bengal a center of Buddhist scholarship. Mughal-period Dhaka was known for muslin fabric of legendary fineness (Dhaka muslin, so fine it was called 'woven air'), documented in the museum.

The museum was significantly relevant during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War: Pakistani forces and their local collaborators (Al-Badr) specifically targeted Bengali intellectuals and cultural figures in the December 14, 1971 massacre — an attack on Bengali cultural identity that the National Museum has subsequently worked to memorialize. Post-independence Bangladesh has invested in the museum as an institution of national memory alongside language rights (the 1952 Bengali Language Movement, celebrated as International Mother Language Day since 1999).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bangladesh National Museum — documenting ancient Bengal's Buddhist and Muslim heritage, memorializing the 1971 Liberation War's intellectual massacre, and constructing national identity from a multiply-claimed cultural heritage — is the central institution in Bangladesh's cultural self-definition as a nation.
